name: Zoe Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Greystone with my husband Owen. It's his family's place: 90 suckler cows and about 250 acres of wheat and barley. Owen's dad Gerald still owns it and still has the final say, even at seventy-two. I run the cattle side, calving, the bull, the sales, and in summer I take our big tractor out contract hedge-cutting and baling silage for the neighbours, which is our own money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, check the cows, feed round in winter, then whatever Gerald's decided needs doing, which isn't always what I'd have chosen. Afternoons I'm often on a neighbour's farm with the hedge cutter. Evenings it's the kids' homework, Bethan's fourteen and Rhys is eleven, and then the paperwork. We've built a bungalow at the bottom of the yard on a mortgage, and we've got maybe three weeks' money if the tractor doesn't break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's a relief, I suppose. One less thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there was a lot of fuss for not much. At the young farmers I'd tell them to learn their stock and their machines, because that's what still counts. I'd be glad it didn't take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, our worries are the same as yesterday: beef prices, the tractor loan, and what happens when Gerald goes. He hasn't made a will that we've seen, and if the farm gets split between Owen and his sisters, we're done. AI was never the big thing for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep the contracting going, maybe add two more hedge-cutting customers. I'd ask Owen to have the talk with his dad about the will this winter. And I'd keep the spray records on the app Owen's cousin showed me, because it does save me an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but about family things more than computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that talk with Gerald go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. Gerald thinks talking about wills is like inviting the undertaker in. My husband Owen is forty-five and still doesn't know if he'll own the farm he's worked all his life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What brings in the contracting money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight thousand pounds a summer, which is our savings, our holiday and the kids' shoes. Without it we'd be living on what Gerald pays us. I'd keep that going whatever happens.

say: I'd say there was **a lot of fuss** for not much.
I'd tell the young farmers to learn their **stock and machines**.
think: I think our worries are **beef prices**, the tractor loan and **Gerald's will**.
If the farm gets **split** between Owen and his sisters, we're done.
do: Add **two more hedge-cutting** customers this summer.
Ask Owen to raise **the will** with his dad this winter.
Keep using the **spray records app** to save an evening.
S0.quote: My husband Owen is forty-five and still doesn't know if he'll own the farm he's worked all his life.
fieldNote: Zoe's main worry is **succession**: no will seen, and the farm could be split.
Her **contracting income** is the household's real savings.
She uses one **app** because it's proven and saves time, typical of her steady approach.
Her **traditional** view shows in pointing young farmers to stock and machines.

steps.text: Take on two more hedge-cutting customers this summer
Get Owen to talk to Gerald about the will this winter
Keep spray records on the app Owen's cousin showed her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and booking and so on. Not much of that on a beef farm, but some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine as long as it doesn't replace hard work. At church and the young farmers I'd tell people to learn it but not lean on it. Hard work and family are still what keep a farm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it might help with the paperwork, and it could help our contracting with bookings. But it'd help the big contractors more, and they'd undercut me on price. If I lose the hedge-cutting customers, I lose our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other contractors are using a booking app, I'd get one too, so customers can book me easily. I'd keep my prices fair and rely on doing a better job than the big firms. And I'd ask Bethan to help me with the online side, she's good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see where it's going but it's not on top of me yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the big contractors undercut you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd plan routes and jobs better with the software, so they can do more farms a day for less. I do a better job, everyone says so, but price is price. Gerald's neighbour switched to the big firm last year to save forty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in learning it but not leaning on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'd say use AI for the forms, not for knowing your cattle. Bethan would tell me I'm old-fashioned, and she'd be half right.

think: I think it helps the **big contractors** more than me.

It could help the contracting a bit with **bookings**, too.
do: Get a **booking app** once other contractors use one.
Keep **prices fair** and compete on doing a better job.
Ask **Bethan** to help with the online side.
feel: **Uneasy**, seeing where it's going but **not on top** of her yet.
S1.quote: I'd say use AI for the forms, not for knowing your cattle.
fieldNote: Zoe's exposure is through **contracting**: bigger firms with better software undercut her.
She'd adopt tools **once others have**, the steady pattern.
Her own daughter would call her **old-fashioned**, and she half agrees.
Losing contracting work could cut the **household savings**, so she's anxious.

steps.text: Set up a booking app for hedge-cutting once rivals have one
Compete on quality with fair prices for silage and hedges
Ask Bethan to run the contracting's online bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and robots in three more. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep family farms going and train young people for real work. I'd want apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd vote for whoever said that and say so at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the contracting's gone by 2031, when robot hedge cutters and balers come. Big contractors would buy them first. And if Gerald sells up or the farm gets split, we'd have nothing and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to push Gerald to sort out the will, no more waiting. I'd take an AI course from the farming union so I can at least run the paperwork side well. And I'd look at getting a robot hedge cutter on finance myself in 2031, with Owen's agreement, if the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a cow down in the field and you can't get her up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do those three years before robots change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the years I'd still have the contracting money. I'd use them to save every penny and decide whether to buy a robot or give it up. After that, the hands-on bit's not safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Bethan and Rhys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Bethan and my son Rhys to learn a trade that needs a person, nursing or electrics or vet work. And I'd tell them family looks after family, whatever happens with the farm.

say: I'd want **apprenticeships**, not handouts, to keep family farms going.
I'd vote for whoever said that and say so **at church**.
think: I think the **contracting's gone** by 2031 when robot cutters arrive.
If the farm is **split or sold**, we'd have nothing and no savings.
do: Push Gerald to **sort the will** in the first year.
Take the farming union's **AI course** for the paperwork side.
Look at a **robot hedge cutter** on finance in 2031.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a **cow down** in the field that won't get up.
S2.quote: Family looks after family, whatever happens with the farm.
fieldNote: Zoe expects to **lose the contracting income** by 2031, which is her savings.
She'd finally force the **will conversation** with her father-in-law.
She'd consider **buying a robot** herself, a big shift for a steady person.
Her advice to her kids is **trades** that need a person and family loyalty.

steps.text: Push Gerald to sign a will in the first year
Take the farming union's AI course for paperwork
Price a robot hedge cutter on finance for 2031
Vote for the party promising farm apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. AGI 2031, robots 2034. I'd be fifty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to train up the young ones properly. I'd push the young farmers to run courses on the new kit. And I'd say families need to sort out their succession now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same worry as the fast one, but with time to fix the will and save some money. Contracting would last until about 2034. I'd have a chance to decide whether to buy a robot or switch to something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see what the big contractors do. Then I'd do the union AI course and look at robot prices. And I'd put a thousand pounds from each summer's contracting into a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have time to think. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change first on Greystone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork and the selling, from 2031. The cattle sales would go through some AI system, and the subsidy forms. Then from 2034, the robots for the hedges and the feeding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd change what I do on the farm before I'd leave it. Farming's not a job for us, it's the family.

I'd say families need to sort **succession** now.
think: I think it's the same worry, but with time to **fix the will** and save.

S3.quote: Farming's not a job for us, it's the family.
fieldNote: Five years lets Zoe **save and plan**, but the contracting income is still at risk.
She'd **wait and watch** first, true to her steady nature.
She'd **change roles** on the farm before ever leaving it.

steps.text: Watch what the big contractors do for a year or two
Do the farming union's AI course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Bethan would be twenty-four. Rhys twenty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives families time to plan, and I'd want the government to stay out of the way and let us. Apprenticeships would help. I'd say it at church and the young farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. Gerald would likely have passed it on, the kids would be grown, and I could build the contracting into a proper business with the new kit. Money would still be tight, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and add tools once they're proven. I'd save from the contracting each year. And I'd encourage Rhys to do an engineering apprenticeship, so he could fix the robots one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Not completely easy, but steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why engineering for Rhys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys is always taking things apart in the shed. If the robots come, someone has to fix them, and I'd rather it was my son than a stranger from the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerald. Ten years or two, the will is still the thing. Robots don't scare me as much as an empty will.

I'd want the government to stay **out of the way** and back apprenticeships.
think: I think ten years feels **manageable**, with the kids grown.
I could build the **contracting** into a proper business.
do: Add **proven tools** each year, once neighbours have tried them.
S4.quote: Robots don't scare me as much as an empty will.
fieldNote: The decade lets Zoe plan **succession** and the contracting business.

steps.text: Add proven farm tools one at a time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The contracting money would go before we'd sorted the will or saved anything. What would help is apprenticeships for young people and a simple way for families to settle succession without a fight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about in-laws. A lot of farms are run by people who don't own them, waiting on a parent's say-so. That's a worry no robot causes and no robot fixes.

headlineQuote: A lot of farms are run by people who don't own them, waiting on a parent's say-so.
portrait: Zoe runs the **cattle** on her in-laws' farm and does **contract hedge-cutting**.
Her household relies on **contracting money** and has three weeks saved.
She's **traditional**, values family and apprenticeships, and uses AI only when proven.
Her deepest worry is **succession**: her father-in-law hasn't shown a will.
She's **alarmed** in the fastest scenario and anxious otherwise.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the **contracting money** goes before the will is settled.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for young people and a simple way to settle **succession**.
